subtopic_detail: targeting the household environment to reduce relapse risk after a first episode of psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an early psychosis service reviewing a 19 year old man six weeks after his first admission. He presented with four months of persecutory beliefs about his neighbours and has responded well to risperidone, with his beliefs now held without conviction and his sleep and appetite restored.

He has moved back in with his parents. In the family meeting his father describes him as lazy and says he could snap out of it if he made an effort, and his mother becomes tearful and says she checks on him several times each night. They argue about his medication most days. Both parents say they are frightened and want to know what they can do. He is taking his medication reliably and is not using substances.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows settled affect, no current perceptual disturbance, residual persecutory ideas held without conviction, insight partially retained, no thoughts of self harm
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on two occasions, adherence confirmed by dose administration aid counts, metabolic screen within normal limits at baseline

lead_in: Which intervention is most likely to reduce his risk of relapse over the next year?

options.text: Referral to a supported employment programme with an individual placement
options.rationale: Individual placement and support improves vocational outcomes and is an important part of early psychosis care, but its demonstrated effect is on employment rather than on relapse. It sits alongside rather than ahead of the family work. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: An increase in the risperidone dose with review in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: He has already responded well at the current dose and is taking it reliably, so there is no pharmacological failure to correct. Raising the dose adds metabolic and extrapyramidal burden, which is itself a common reason young people stop medication and relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Addition of an antidepressant to target his negative symptoms and low mood
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a limited and inconsistent effect on negative symptoms, and no depressive syndrome has been described here. Adding a second psychotropic without a clear indication complicates the regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Referral of the patient alone for individual cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Individual cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis is recommended and helps residual symptoms and distress, so this is a genuine component of good care rather than a wrong treatment. It does not address the household environment, which is the specific modifiable factor operating here. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: A structured family intervention with psychoeducation and communication skills
options.rationale: Households with high levels of criticism, hostility or emotional overinvolvement carry a substantially higher relapse rate, and the pattern described in this meeting fits both the critical and the overinvolved forms. Structured family work delivered over several months reduces relapse and readmission by roughly half, an effect size comparable to maintenance medication. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Expressed emotion describes the level of criticism, hostility and emotional overinvolvement directed toward a family member with a psychotic illness, and it is one of the most consistently replicated predictors of relapse, with relapse rates in high expressed emotion households roughly double those in low expressed emotion households over the year following discharge. The concept is not about blame: families arrive at these patterns through fear and exhaustion, and attributions such as laziness usually reflect a lack of information about negative symptoms rather than indifference. Structured family intervention combines psychoeducation about the illness and its treatment, communication skills training, structured problem solving and crisis planning, delivered over at least six months and generally around ten or more sessions. Meta analyses show reductions in relapse and readmission of about half, which places it among the most effective single interventions available in early psychosis and is why it is recommended for every family in contact with a first episode service. It works alongside maintenance antipsychotic medication, individual psychological therapy and vocational support rather than replacing any of them.
key_points: High expressed emotion roughly doubles relapse rates over the first year
Criticism, hostility and emotional overinvolvement are the three components
Attributions such as laziness usually reflect misunderstanding of negative symptoms
Structured family intervention runs over at least six months and around ten sessions
Relapse and readmission fall by approximately half
explanation.pearls: Ask a carer what they think causes the person's inactivity: an answer framed as a character flaw rather than an illness feature identifies high expressed emotion at the bedside and predicts relapse more reliably than any symptom rating scale.

subtopic_detail: recording treatment preferences while a person retains capacity for use during future episodes of illness
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman on the ward. She has bipolar affective disorder and has had three admissions with mania over eight years, on each occasion declining lithium while unwell and accepting it again once she recovered.

She came in voluntarily ten days ago with early elevation of mood, which has now settled. She is sleeping normally, her speech is unpressured and she describes her mood as back to her usual self. She tells you she hates that decisions get made for her when she is unwell and asks how she can have a say in her own treatment next time. She understands her diagnosis, can describe what happens when she becomes unwell, and weighs up the options you discuss with her.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows euthymic mood, normal rate and form of speech, no grandiosity, no perceptual disturbance, insight intact, decision making capacity retained on assessment
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium level within the therapeutic range, thyroid function within normal limits, renal function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Support her to complete an advance statement of her treatment preferences
options.rationale: An advance statement is made while a person has capacity and records the treatment they would want, and would not want, if they later become unwell and lose it. Australian mental health legislation requires treating teams to consider such a statement and to give written reasons when they depart from it, so completing it now is the action that gives her genuine influence over future episodes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Apply now for a community treatment order to cover any future episode
options.rationale: A compulsory order can only be made when the statutory criteria are met at the time, which requires a current mental illness with the person unable to consent and a risk that cannot be addressed less restrictively. She is well and consenting, and a pre-emptive order is not lawful. (Source: Mental Health Act frameworks for Australian states and territories)
source_refs: Mental Health Act frameworks for Australian states and territories

options.text: Apply to the tribunal for a guardian to be appointed to make decisions
options.rationale: Guardianship transfers decision making away from the person and is reserved for those with enduring incapacity, usually from cognitive impairment or disability. Her incapacity is episodic and she currently has capacity, so this is a disproportionate response that achieves the opposite of what she is asking for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Record her wishes in the file and review them at her next admission
options.rationale: A file note carries no standing under mental health legislation and may not be found by a team meeting her in an emergency. The statutory instrument exists precisely so that her wishes carry weight rather than depending on whether someone reads the notes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Ask her family to make future treatment decisions on her behalf
options.rationale: Nominating a support person is a legitimate and valuable part of this planning, but a nominated person supports the individual to express their own will and preferences rather than substituting their judgement. Handing the decision to family bypasses her stated wishes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Australian mental health legislation has moved from a substitute decision making model toward supported decision making, reflecting obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The practical instruments that express this are the advance statement of preferences, made while the person has capacity and setting out the treatment they would and would not want in a future episode, and the nominated support person, who is appointed to help the person express their own will and preferences rather than to decide on their behalf. Treating teams must consider an advance statement and, in most jurisdictions, must record written reasons if compulsory treatment departs from it, which means the document shapes clinical decisions even though it does not bind them absolutely. The clinical value extends beyond the legal effect: the conversation itself identifies which aspects of previous admissions the person found most distressing, such as seclusion, a particular medication or the involvement of police, and often surfaces workable alternatives. Recovery oriented practice treats episodes of incapacity as interruptions in an ongoing relationship with an autonomous person rather than as a licence to disregard their preferences.
key_points: Advance statements are made while capacity is retained for use during later incapacity
Teams must consider the statement and usually give written reasons for departing from it
A nominated support person assists expression of the person's own preferences
Compulsory orders require the statutory criteria to be met at the time, not in advance
The planning conversation surfaces workable alternatives to distressing past interventions
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically which part of a previous admission the person found most distressing and what helped: answers such as a preference for olanzapine over haloperidol, or for a particular relative to be called before police, are exactly what an advance statement can make binding on the team's reasoning.

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for repetitive hair pulling presenting as patchy scalp hair loss
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 16 year old girl referred by a dermatologist. Her parents brought her to the dermatologist three months ago because of patchy hair loss on her scalp and were told it was probably an autoimmune condition.

The dermatologist found broken hairs of many different lengths within the patches, no scaling and no smooth complete bald areas, with normal skin throughout, and a fungal scraping was negative. Seen alone, she tells you she pulls hairs out one at a time while studying and while watching television, often without noticing at first. She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, says she has tried many times to stop, and is embarrassed about how her hair looks at school.

data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches of hair loss over the right parietal scalp containing broken hairs of varying lengths, no scaling, no erythema, no exclamation mark hairs, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no other skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Fungal scraping negative, full blood count within normal limits, iron studies within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at an antidepressant dose
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder itself but trials in hair pulling have been largely negative, which is one of the features that separates this condition from obsessive compulsive disorder despite their grouping together. It may still be used where a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Habit reversal training delivered by a trained psychologist
options.rationale: Behavioural treatment combining awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control has the strongest evidence for this condition and is recommended ahead of medication. Awareness training matters particularly here because much of her pulling is automatic and outside her attention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Oral N acetylcysteine at high dose with review in three months
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine has some supportive trial evidence in adults and is reasonably well tolerated, which makes it a recognised second line option. The evidence in adolescents is weaker and it is not used ahead of the behavioural treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Potent topical corticosteroid applied to the affected scalp areas
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats alopecia areata, which is the diagnosis she was originally given, and the two are separated by the examination findings. Areata produces smooth complete bald patches with tapered exclamation mark hairs, whereas broken hairs of differing lengths within an irregular patch indicate mechanical extraction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Low dose olanzapine with monitoring of weight and metabolic profile
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has been trialled in refractory cases but carries substantial metabolic risk in an adolescent. It is not a first line treatment for a condition with an effective and well tolerated behavioural option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified among the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and is defined by recurrent pulling of one's own hair resulting in hair loss, with repeated attempts to stop and associated distress or impairment. Onset is typically in early adolescence and it is considerably more common in females presenting to clinics. Pulling occurs in two modes that often coexist: a focused mode preceded by mounting tension and followed by relief or gratification, and an automatic mode occurring outside awareness during sedentary activities such as reading or screen time, which is why awareness training is a necessary first component of treatment. The distinction from alopecia areata rests on the appearance of the patches, since mechanical pulling leaves hairs broken at varying lengths within an irregularly shaped area of otherwise normal scalp, whereas areata produces smooth complete loss with tapered exclamation mark hairs. Trichophagia should be asked about directly because swallowed hair can form a gastric trichobezoar with a tail extending into the small bowel, a rare but surgically important complication.
key_points: Broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular patch indicate pulling, not alopecia areata
Pulling occurs in both focused and automatic modes, often in the same person
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Serotonergic antidepressants have largely negative trial evidence for this condition
Ask directly about swallowing hair because of the risk of a gastric trichobezoar
explanation.pearls: Always ask whether the person swallows the hair they pull, because a trichobezoar with a tail extending through the pylorus into the jejunum presents with vomiting and weight loss and requires surgical removal rather than any psychiatric treatment.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
